nodes.name: A probability is a number from 0 to 1
nodes.statement: The probability of a chance event is a number from 0 to 1 that expresses how likely the event is: 0 for an impossible event, 1 for a certain event, and larger numbers for more likely events.
nodes.assess: Which of these numbers could be the probability of an event: 0.7, 4/3, 0, -0.2, 1, 1/5?

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem asks whether 0.7 lies from 0 to 1, which compares a decimal with the whole numbers 0 and 1.
The test problem lists 0.7 as a possible probability, which is read as 7 tenths and so lies between 0 and 1.
The statement places probabilities such as 1/5 as numbers on a scale from 0 to 1, so a fraction must already be a number.
The test problem asks whether 4/3 can be a probability, which needs seeing that 4/3 is greater than 1.
Ruling out -0.2 in the test problem needs negative numbers to lie left of 0 on the number line and so be less than 0.
The test problem lists -0.2, a negative number on the opposite side of 0 from every probability, so it is ruled out.

nodes.name: Interpret a probability as unlikely, neither, or likely
nodes.statement: A probability near 0 describes an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 a likely event; of two events, the one with the larger probability is the more likely.
nodes.assess: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.9, the probability of snow is 0.05, and the probability a tossed coin lands heads is 1/2. Describe each event as unlikely, neither unlikely nor likely, or likely. Which of the three is most likely?

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem gives 0.9 and 0.05 and asks which event is most likely, which compares these two decimals.
Deciding whether a probability is near 0, around 1/2, or near 1 compares a fraction with benchmark fractions.
The statement reads a probability as a number on the 0 to 1 scale of likelihood, with 0 impossible and 1 certain.

nodes.name: Estimate a probability by the relative frequency over many trials
nodes.statement: The probability of a chance event is approximated by its relative frequency after many trials of the chance process: the number of trials in which the event occurred divided by the number of trials.
nodes.assess: A thumbtack was tossed 200 times and landed point up 120 times. Estimate the probability that the thumbtack lands point up.
procedure: Repeat the chance process many times and record whether the event occurs in each trial.
Count the trials in which the event occurred.
Divide that count by the number of trials.

proposed_edges.rationale: Counting the trials in which the event occurred means counting the trials in each category, event or not event.
Step 3 divides the count of trials with the event by the number of trials, which is written as the fraction count over trials.
The statement approximates a probability, a number from 0 to 1 measuring likelihood, by a relative frequency of trials.

nodes.name: More trials give a more reliable probability estimate
nodes.statement: As the number of trials of a chance process grows, the relative frequency of an event tends to get closer to its probability; with few trials it can be far from the probability.
nodes.assess: Ana tossed a paper cup 10 times and Ben tossed the same cup 500 times, each to estimate the probability that it lands on its side. Their estimates differ. Whose estimate is more likely to be close to the actual probability, and why?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement is about how the relative frequency over a number of trials approaches the probability, so relative frequency as an estimate is used.

nodes.name: Predict about how often an event will occur from its probability
nodes.statement: If an event has probability p, then in n trials it is expected to occur about p x n times, and the actual number will usually be close to p x n but not exactly equal to it.
nodes.assess: The probability of rolling a 3 or a 6 on a number cube is 1/3. In 600 rolls, about how many times would you expect a 3 or a 6? Would you expect exactly that many?

proposed_edges.rationale: Finding p x n for a fractional probability such as 1/3 and n = 600 multiplies a fraction by a whole number.
Expecting about p x n occurrences uses the relative frequency, count over n, being close to the probability p but not equal to it.
The claim that the actual number is usually close to p x n but not exactly equal rests on relative frequency varying around the probability.

nodes.name: Develop a uniform probability model
nodes.statement: When the outcomes of a chance process are equally likely, a uniform probability model lists all n possible outcomes and assigns each one the probability 1/n.
nodes.assess: Spinner 1 has 5 equal sections labeled A, B, C, D, E. List the outcomes of one spin and give the probability of each. Spinner 2 has 3 sections, one of which is half of the circle. Would a uniform model fit spinner 2? Why or why not?

proposed_edges.rationale: The probability assigned to each of n equally likely outcomes is written as the unit fraction 1/n, one of n equal parts.
The model assigns each outcome a probability, a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely that outcome is.

nodes.name: Find the probability of an event in a uniform model
nodes.statement: In a uniform probability model, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the total number of outcomes.
nodes.assess: A student is selected at random from a class of 12 girls and 13 boys. What is the probability that a girl is selected?
procedure: Count the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Count the outcomes that make up the event.
Divide the number of outcomes in the event by the total number of outcomes.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem needs the class total 12 + 13 to get the number of equally likely outcomes.
Counting the total number of equally likely outcomes, and the outcomes in the event, is counting a collection.
Step 3 divides the number of outcomes in the event by the total number of outcomes, written as the fraction event over total.
The statement works inside a uniform probability model, whose list of n equally likely outcomes supplies the total in the division.

nodes.name: Develop a probability model from observed frequencies
nodes.statement: A probability model, which need not be uniform, is developed from data on a chance process by assigning each outcome its observed relative frequency; comparing these values shows whether the outcomes appear equally likely.
nodes.assess: A paper cup was tossed 100 times. It landed on its side 70 times, open end up 20 times, and open end down 10 times. Give an approximate probability for each outcome. Do the three outcomes appear equally likely?
procedure: Record how many times each outcome occurred in many trials.
Divide each count by the total number of trials to get each outcome's relative frequency.
Assign each outcome its relative frequency as its approximate probability.
Compare the probabilities to judge whether the outcomes appear equally likely.

proposed_edges.rationale: Recording how many times each outcome occurred is counting the trials in each category.
Step 4 judges whether outcomes appear equally likely, using the meaning of equally likely outcomes that share the same probability.
Steps 2 and 3 find each outcome's relative frequency by the same count over trials division used to estimate one probability.

nodes.name: Find the probability of an event in a model whose outcomes are not equally likely
nodes.statement: When a probability model gives outcomes different probabilities, the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes that make it up, not the number of those outcomes divided by the number of outcomes.
nodes.assess: A spinner's model gives P(red) = 0.5, P(blue) = 0.3, and P(green) = 0.2. What is the probability that the spinner lands on red or green?
procedure: List the outcomes that make up the event.
Read the probability of each of those outcomes from the model.
Add those probabilities.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem adds P(red) = 0.5 and P(green) = 0.2, which is a sum of two decimals.
A probability model that lists outcomes with their probabilities is first set up in the uniform model, which this statement then generalizes.
The statement treats an event as the outcomes that make it up and contrasts its sum rule with the count over total rule for uniform models.

nodes.name: Represent the sample space of a compound event with an organized list
nodes.statement: The sample space of a compound event is the set of all possible combinations of outcomes of its stages; an organized list records every combination once by fixing the outcome of the first stage and running through all outcomes of the later stages before changing it.
nodes.assess: A spinner with equal sections labeled 1, 2, and 3 is spun twice. Make an organized list of all possible outcomes.

proposed_edges.rationale: The sample space combines the outcomes of each stage, and listing all the possible outcomes of one chance process is set up in the uniform model node.

nodes.name: Represent the sample space of a two-stage compound event with a table
nodes.statement: For a compound event with two stages, a table whose rows are the outcomes of the first stage and whose columns are the outcomes of the second stage has one cell for each outcome in the sample space.
nodes.assess: A coin is tossed and a number cube is rolled. Make a table that shows every possible outcome.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement counts one cell per outcome in the sample space, the set of all combinations of stage outcomes defined with the organized list.
The statement is stated in a table whose rows are first-stage outcomes and columns second-stage outcomes, with one cell per outcome.

nodes.name: Represent the sample space of a compound event with a tree diagram
nodes.statement: A tree diagram for a compound event branches once for each outcome of the first stage and then, from the end of every branch, once for each outcome of the next stage; each path from the start to the end of a last branch is one outcome in the sample space.
nodes.assess: A coin is tossed three times. Draw a tree diagram that shows every possible outcome.

proposed_edges.rationale: Each path of the tree is one outcome in the sample space, the set of all combinations of stage outcomes defined with the organized list.

nodes.name: Identify the outcomes that make up a compound event
nodes.statement: For a compound event described in everyday language, the outcomes that make it up are exactly the outcomes in the sample space for which the description is true.
nodes.assess: Two number cubes are rolled. The sample space is the 36 ordered pairs (first cube, second cube), shown in a 6-by-6 table. List all the outcomes that make up the event 'at least one cube shows a 6'.
procedure: Write or read the full sample space.
Check each outcome against the description of the event.
List the outcomes for which the description is true.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement picks the outcomes that make up an event from the sample space, the set of all combinations of the stages' outcomes.
The test problem gives the sample space of two number cubes as a 6-by-6 table in which each cell is one outcome.

nodes.name: The probability of a compound event as a fraction of the sample space
nodes.statement: When the outcomes in the sample space of a compound event are equally likely, the probability of the event is the number of outcomes in which it occurs divided by the number of outcomes in the sample space, just as for a simple event.
nodes.assess: Two fair coins are tossed. The sample space is HH, HT, TH, TT. Sam says the probability of exactly one head is 1/3, because the result can be 0 heads, 1 head, or 2 heads. What is the probability of exactly one head, and what is wrong with Sam's reasoning?

proposed_edges.rationale: The numerator counts the outcomes in which the compound event occurs, found by checking each outcome against the event's description.
Explaining Sam's error uses that 0, 1 and 2 heads are not equally likely outcomes, unlike the four outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT.
The statement says the probability is outcomes in the event over outcomes in the sample space 'just as for a simple event', the uniform rule.
The denominator is the number of outcomes in the sample space of the compound event, defined in the list node.

nodes.name: Design a simulation for a compound event
nodes.statement: A simulation for a compound event uses a random device whose outcomes have the same probabilities as each stage of the real process, and states what one trial is and how to tell from a trial whether the event occurred.
nodes.assess: 40% of blood donors have type A blood. Design a simulation with random digits 0 to 9 for finding donors one at a time until one has type A blood. Say which digits stand for type A, what one trial is, and how to tell whether a trial needed at least 4 donors.
procedure: Choose a random device, such as random digits, a spinner, or a number cube, and assign its outcomes so that each stage's outcomes have the right probabilities.
Define one trial as the sequence of draws that plays out the whole compound process once.
State the rule that decides from a trial's draws whether the event occurred.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem gives 40% and asks how many of the 10 digits should stand for type A, which is 40% of 10.
The test problem gives the probability as 40%, which must be read as 40 per 100 and turned into 4 of the 10 digits.
Step 3 states a rule that decides whether a trial's draws satisfy the event's description, which is checking an outcome against that description.
Step 1 assigns k of n equally likely digits to an outcome so that its probability is k over n, as in a uniform model.

nodes.name: Estimate the probability of a compound event from simulation results
nodes.statement: Given the results of a simulation and its rule for when the compound event occurs, decide for each trial whether the event occurred and estimate the probability as the fraction of trials in which it did.
nodes.assess: In a simulation, digits 0 to 3 stand for a donor with type A blood and digits 4 to 9 for a donor without; each trial reads digits until the first 0 to 3. Ten trials gave: 2, 71, 9550, 861, 0, 47943, 3, 52, 6681, 91. Estimate the probability that at least 4 donors are needed to find one with type A blood.
procedure: For each trial, apply the rule to decide whether the compound event occurred.
Count the trials in which the event occurred.
Divide that count by the number of trials.

proposed_edges.rationale: Applying the rule to each trial checks that trial's outcome against the description of the compound event.
Steps 2 and 3 count the trials in which the event occurred and divide by the number of trials, the relative frequency estimate itself.

nodes.name: Make a scatter plot of bivariate measurement data
nodes.statement: A scatter plot shows data on two quantities measured on the same individuals by plotting, for each individual, the point whose coordinates are its two values, one variable on each axis, without connecting the points.
nodes.assess: Make a scatter plot of hours studied (x) and test score (y) for six students: (1, 60), (2, 65), (3, 70), (4, 72), (5, 80), (6, 85).
procedure: Choose which variable goes on the horizontal axis and which on the vertical axis.
Scale each axis to cover the range of that variable's values.
For each individual, plot the point (first value, second value).

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 plots the point (first value, second value) for each individual, which is plotting a point with whole-number coordinates in the first quadrant.
Step 2 chooses and marks a scale on each axis that covers the range of the values, as when choosing the scale of a bar graph.

nodes.name: Positive, negative, and no association in a scatter plot
nodes.statement: Two quantities have a positive association when larger values of one tend to go with larger values of the other, a negative association when larger values of one tend to go with smaller values of the other, and no association when there is no such tendency; a tendency allows individual exceptions.
nodes.assess: In a scatter plot of hours of practice (x) and free throws missed (y) for 20 players, the points fall from the upper left to the lower right, though a few players who practiced more missed more than some who practiced less. Is the association positive, negative, or none? What does it say about practice and missed free throws?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement describes tendencies shown by a scatter plot, where each point is a pair of values of the two quantities.

nodes.name: Linear and nonlinear association
nodes.statement: An association shown in a scatter plot is linear when the points lie roughly along a straight line and nonlinear when they follow a curve.
nodes.assess: Data set A: (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 6), (4, 9), (5, 11). Data set B: (0, 9), (1, 4), (2, 1), (3, 0), (4, 1), (5, 4), (6, 9). Plot each. Which shows a linear association and which a nonlinear association?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement classifies the pattern of points in a scatter plot, and the test problem asks for both data sets to be plotted.
A linear association is one whose points lie roughly along a straight line, so the idea of a straight line is used.

nodes.name: Strong and weak linear association
nodes.statement: A linear association is strong when the points lie close to a line and weak when they are widely scattered about it; strength is separate from direction.
nodes.assess: Two scatter plots both show a positive linear association. In plot A every point is within 1 unit of a line through the data; in plot B many points are 10 or more units from any line through the data. Which shows the stronger association?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement says strength is separate from direction, and the test problem gives two plots that have the same positive direction.
Strength is defined only for a linear association, whose points lie roughly along a straight line, so the statement uses that idea.

nodes.name: Clusters and outliers in a scatter plot
nodes.statement: In a scatter plot, a cluster is a group of points lying close together and separated from the other points by a gap, and an outlier is a point lying far from the overall pattern of the others.
nodes.assess: A scatter plot shows the points (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (8, 9), (9, 10), (10, 11), and (5, 15). Name the clusters and the outlier.

proposed_edges.rationale: Clusters and outliers are groups and single points in a scatter plot, where each point is a pair of values from one individual.
An outlier is a point far from the overall pattern, which is the striking deviation from a pattern described in that node.

nodes.name: A straight line can model bivariate data with a linear association
nodes.statement: When a scatter plot shows a linear association, a straight line can model the relationship between the two quantities by summarizing their trend; the data points need not lie on the line.
nodes.assess: A scatter plot of arm span against height for 25 students shows a strong positive linear association, but no straight line passes through all the points. Tom says this means a straight line cannot be used to model the data. Is he right? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement applies when a scatter plot shows a linear association, which is points lying roughly along a straight line.

nodes.name: Informally fit a straight line to a scatter plot
nodes.statement: For a scatter plot that suggests a linear association, draw a straight line that follows the trend of the points, with the points as close to the line as possible and roughly as many above it as below it along its length.
nodes.assess: Plot the points (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 6), (5, 8), (6, 9) and draw a straight line that fits the data.
procedure: Judge the direction of the trend from the points.
Place a straight edge along the trend so that the points are as close to it as possible.
Adjust it until roughly as many points lie above it as below it, at both ends and in the middle.
Draw the line across the range of the data.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 judges from the points whether the trend rises or falls, which is deciding positive or negative association.
The test problem asks for the six given points to be plotted as a scatter plot before the line is drawn.
The line drawn is the line that models the trend, summarizing the data without having to pass through every point.

nodes.name: Judge the fit of a line by the closeness of the points to it
nodes.statement: A line fits a data set well when the data points lie close to it, with no long run of points all on one side; the farther the points lie from the line, the worse the fit.
nodes.assess: Two lines are drawn on the same scatter plot. Line A passes above all but one of the points, some by as much as 4 units. Line B passes through the middle of the points, with about half above and half below, each within 1 unit of it. Which line fits the data better? Explain using the distances of the points from the lines.

proposed_edges.rationale: Judging how well a line fits uses the idea of a line that models the trend of the data without passing through every point.

nodes.name: Interpret the slope of a line fitted to data
nodes.statement: The slope of a line fitted to bivariate data is the predicted change in the second quantity for each increase of one unit in the first, in units of the second per unit of the first; it describes the trend of the data, not the exact change for every individual.
nodes.assess: A line fitted to data on hours of sunlight per day (x) and mature plant height in cm (y) is y = 1.5x + 10. What does the slope 1.5 mean in this context?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement says the slope describes the trend of the data, not the exact change for each individual, which uses the line as a model.
The test problem gives y = 1.5x + 10 and asks about the slope 1.5, so the learner must see the coefficient of x as the slope.
The slope is read as the change in the second quantity per one unit of the first, the rate of change of a linear model in context.

nodes.name: Interpret the intercept of a line fitted to data
nodes.statement: The vertical intercept of a line fitted to bivariate data is the value of the second quantity that the model predicts when the first quantity is 0; the prediction may be meaningless when 0 lies far outside the data.
nodes.assess: A line fitted to data on hours of sunlight per day (x) and mature plant height in cm (y) is y = 1.5x + 10. What does the intercept 10 mean in this context?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement calls the intercept a prediction by the line, one that may be meaningless far outside the data, which uses the line as a model.
The test problem gives y = 1.5x + 10 and asks about the intercept 10, so the learner must see the constant term as the value at x = 0.
The intercept is read as the value of the second quantity when the first is 0, the initial value of a linear model in context.

nodes.name: Predict a value from the equation of a line fitted to data
nodes.statement: Problems that give the equation of a line fitted to bivariate data and a value of the first quantity, and ask for the value of the second quantity that the model predicts; the answer is a prediction from the trend, not an exact value for any individual.
nodes.assess: A line fitted to data on hours of sunlight per day (x) and mature plant height in cm (y) is y = 1.5x + 10. Predict the mature height of a plant that gets 6 hours of sunlight a day.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem evaluates 1.5 x 6 + 10 after substituting, which is a numerical expression with a decimal.
Finding the predicted value substitutes the given value of the first quantity into the equation and evaluates it.
The statement says the answer is a prediction from the trend and not an exact value for any individual, which uses the line as a model.

nodes.name: Find the input a fitted line associates with a given output
nodes.statement: Problems that give the equation of a line fitted to bivariate data and a value of the second quantity, and ask for the value of the first quantity that the model associates with it, found by solving the equation for the first quantity.
nodes.assess: A line fitted to data on hours of sunlight per day (x) and mature plant height in cm (y) is y = 1.5x + 10. According to the model, about how many hours of sunlight a day go with a mature height of 25 cm?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement finds the first quantity by solving the equation for it, and the test problem solves 1.5x + 10 = 25.
The input the model associates with an output is a value read from a line that summarizes the trend, not an exact value.

nodes.name: Construct a two-way table from data on two categorical variables
nodes.statement: A two-way table summarizes data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects: the categories of one variable label the rows, the categories of the other label the columns, each cell holds the number of subjects in both its row category and its column category, and the row totals, column totals, and grand total are written at the margins.
nodes.assess: Ten students answered two questions, 'Do you have a curfew?' and 'Do you have chores?'. Their answers (curfew, chores) were: (yes, yes), (yes, yes), (yes, no), (no, yes), (no, no), (yes, yes), (no, no), (no, yes), (yes, yes), (no, no). Make a two-way table of the counts with row and column totals.
procedure: Label one row for each category of the first variable and one column for each category of the second variable.
For each subject, add one to the cell for that subject's pair of categories.
Add across each row and down each column to write the row and column totals, and add all the cells for the grand total.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 adds across each row and down each column and adds all the cells for the grand total, which are sums of whole numbers.
Step 2 tallies the subjects falling in each pair of categories, which is counting the objects in each category.
The table is laid out with a row for each category of one variable and a column for each of the other, with a cell where they meet.
The statement says what each cell, row total, column total, and grand total of the table counts, which is the meaning of the cells and totals.

nodes.name: What the cells and totals of a two-way table count
nodes.statement: In a two-way table of two categorical variables, a cell counts the subjects that are in both its row category and its column category, a row or column total counts the subjects in that one category whatever their other category, and the grand total counts all the subjects.
nodes.assess: A two-way table has rows 'curfew: yes' and 'curfew: no' and columns 'chores: yes' and 'chores: no'. Row 'curfew: yes' reads 16, 4, total 20. Row 'curfew: no' reads 6, 14, total 20. The column totals are 22 and 18, and the grand total is 40. What does the 4 mean? What does the column total 22 mean?

proposed_edges.rationale: A row or column total counts the subjects in one category, which is the count of a category read from a chart.
The grand total counts all the subjects, which is the total number of data points in the table.
The statement is about what the entries and totals of a table of rows and columns count, so reading an entry by its row and column is used.

nodes.name: Find row or column relative frequencies in a two-way table
nodes.statement: A row relative frequency is a cell count divided by the total of its row, and a column relative frequency is a cell count divided by the total of its column; the row relative frequencies in any one row add to 1, as do the column relative frequencies in any one column.
nodes.assess: A two-way table has rows 'curfew: yes' (16 with chores, 4 without, total 20) and 'curfew: no' (6 with chores, 14 without, total 20). Find the row relative frequencies for the row 'curfew: yes'.
procedure: Choose whether to compare rows or columns.
For rows, divide each cell count by the total of its row; for columns, divide each cell count by the total of its column.
Write each result as a fraction, decimal, or percent.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement claims the relative frequencies in one row add to 1, which adds fractions with the same denominator, the row total.
Step 2 divides each cell count by the total of its row or column, which is written as the fraction cell over total.
The statement divides a cell count by its row or column total, so what a cell and a total count must be known.

nodes.name: Association between two categorical variables
nodes.statement: Two categorical variables are associated when the relative frequencies of the categories of one variable differ from one category of the other variable to the next; when the row (or column) relative frequencies are about the same in every row (or column), the data show no association, however the raw counts differ.
nodes.assess: Table A: of 40 students with a curfew, 30 have chores (75%); of 20 students without a curfew, 15 have chores (75%). Table B: of 20 students with a curfew, 16 have chores (80%); of 20 students without a curfew, 6 have chores (30%). Which table shows an association between having a curfew and having chores? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement defines association by whether row or column relative frequencies differ from one category to the next.

nodes.name: Use relative frequencies in a two-way table to describe an association
nodes.statement: Problems that give a two-way table of counts for two categorical variables and ask whether the data suggest an association, answered by comparing row (or column) relative frequencies and describing the association, if any, in context.
nodes.assess: Of 30 students with a curfew, 24 have chores and 6 do not. Of 10 students without a curfew, 3 have chores and 7 do not. Is there evidence that students who have a curfew also tend to have chores? Support your answer with relative frequencies.

proposed_edges.rationale: The answer decides whether there is an association by judging whether the relative frequencies differ between categories.
The statement says the answer is found by computing row or column relative frequencies from the counts in the two-way table.
